inputs.trimmedTo: the six names this fixture is built around: 4 of the 503 in Components, which is tonight's snapshot and holds no departed name, and all 6 of the 822 in HistoricalTickerComponents, which is where the spans are. Four are current members and two have left, on different dates, so a past-date query has a stretch to answer differently from tonight rather than one leave at the end of the record. The provider's keys are kept as sent, so the gaps in them show where the cut was made. General is whole and every field, nesting and type is the provider's. Recaptured at 3.6 to widen the fixture to four names: the whole file is this one capture rather than the earlier one with a row spliced in, so no row here came from a payload another row did not. The index weights moved a few hundredths between the two captures, which nothing in the pipeline reads and which is the drift a weight is.

nothing. The whole capture, which is the fourth name 3.6 widens the fixture to and the one chosen for character rather than for size. Its year holds a ten for one split on 2025-11-17, so every bar before it is adjusted by a factor of a tenth and the adjustment path is exercised over a whole series rather than over the fractions of a percent a dividend moves. It also holds four sessions that moved more than seven percent from the close before them, which is the gapping character the phase table asks for, and after adjustment it trades between 65 and 127 against ranges of 245 to 345, 350 to 520 and 155 to 375, so the four names differ in price scale as well as in width.

eight of the 44,575 rows the whole US exchange returned, chosen so the membership filter has each thing it must reject. Four are current members and are stored: AAPL, MSFT, NFLX and KEYS. Two are constituents that have left, AAL and XRAY, which the provider still returns because they still trade, and which prove the filter reads membership rather than the file. Two, A and AA, were never in this fixture's index at all. The session is 2026-09-08, which is the next trading session after the stored year ends on 2026-09-04, the Monday between them being a holiday, so appending it leaves a contiguous series and a fetcher that dropped it would be visible as a gap rather than as a shorter year. Rows keep the order the provider sent them in, and every key, nesting and type is the provider's. Recaptured at 3.6 with the session asked for by date rather than as the last day, because the fourth name needed a row for the same session and a file holding rows from two captures is a file whose provenance is per row. The provider's figures for that session had settled between the two fetches: six of the seven earlier rows carry a revised volume or a revised low, which is what a fetchedAt on a capture is for.

the same capture as bars-KEYS.json with one interior session removed, 2026-03-06, which AAPL and MSFT both hold. It is a subset rather than a second capture: every row it keeps is the provider's, byte for byte, and the file exists because a clean provider series will not produce the failure 1.5's done condition requires be induced. The session removed sits in the middle of the window with stored sessions on both sides of it, because a hole at either edge is a shorter history rather than a gap.

four of the 124 rows the whole US exchange returned for that session. AAPL is one of them and its ex-dividend date is a real action inside the stored year, which is what makes the refetch fire on a captured action rather than a constructed one. The other three are names this index does not hold, so the membership filter has something to reject. The date was chosen by reading AAPL's own dividend history first, because a day picked at random holds no action for any fixture name. Every key, nesting and type is the provider's, including the four fields that arrive as null.

three of the eight rows the whole US exchange returned for that session. None is a fixture name, which is deliberate: the split file is here for its shape rather than for its actions, and the shape is the thing a parser written first gets wrong. A split's value is a ratio in a string, and the exchange is under `exchange` where the price bulk file calls the same thing `exchange_short_name`.

four of the articles one name's fortnight returned, kept in the provider's order. Four rather than one because the parser has to be exercised over a row naming several tickers, which is what makes one dated request serve every name; three of the four name three or more. Every key, nesting and type is the provider's. The whole set of thirty names this response came from is the 1.7 coverage measurement's sample and is recorded in PROGRESS.md rather than committed, because 1,253 articles of licensed text are not this repository's to hold.

the whole payload's shape with its rows cut: every one of the thirteen top level keys, every nested key and every type is the provider's, and what was removed is rows. Eight quarters of each of the three statements out of 164, three years of each, eight of the 132 earnings history rows, four of the 40 estimate trend rows, four of the 33 annual rows, two holders of each kind and four share counts of each span. Eight quarters rather than five, because the numbers section shows five reported quarters and one guided, and a file holding exactly six could not show that the fetcher selects rather than storing whatever it was handed. General, Highlights, Valuation, SharesStats, Technicals, SplitsDividends, AnalystRatings, ESGScores and InsiderTransactions are whole. The endpoint carries no segment table and no management guidance at all, which is what the probe settled and why the numbers section marks both absent until the filings archive supplies them.

the same cut as fundamentals-AAPL.json. Its fiscal year ends in June, so its quarter ends do not line up with AAPL's September, which is what a reader ordering five quarters by the calendar rather than per name would get wrong.

the same cut as fundamentals-AAPL.json with one row kept on purpose: the quarter ending 2012-10-31, which the provider files with no filing date at all. It is the only such row in the four captures, and this table's grain is one row per filing date, so a fetcher that required the field would throw on a real name and one that defaulted it would key a row on a date nobody filed. Nine quarters rather than eight for that reason. This name also files no guided quarter: every one of its earnings history rows carries an actual, where the other three each carry one row with an estimate and no actual, so the absence of a guided quarter is in the fixture beside its presence. Its fiscal year ends in October and its most recent quarter was filed on 2026-09-02, which is inside this fixture's own window.
the same cut as fundamentals-AAPL.json. Its fiscal year ends in December, which with AAPL's September, MSFT's June and KEYS's October gives four fiscal calendars over four names.
